title: Text Encoding: ASCII, Unicode, UTF-8 and UTF-16
oneLiner: Characters are numbers called code points, encodings turn them into bytes, and that is why "string length" has three different answers.
keyTakeaway: Unicode assigns every character a code point, a number from U+0000 to U+10FFFF. An encoding turns code points into bytes: UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes and keeps ASCII unchanged, UTF-16 uses one or two 16-bit code units. C#, Java and JavaScript strings are UTF-16, so Length counts code units: "👍".Length is 2. What a user sees as one character (a grapheme cluster) can be several code points, so reversing or truncating a string by index can split an emoji or detach an accent.
explanation:
ASCII (1963) maps 128 characters to the numbers 0 to 127: English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes such as newline (10). It fits in 7 bits. Dozens of incompatible 8-bit code pages then used the values 128 to 255 for other alphabets, which is where garbled text like "Ã©" comes from: bytes written in one encoding and read in another.

Unicode fixes the numbering for every writing system at once. Each character gets a code point, written U+ and at least four hex digits: A is U+0041, é is U+00E9, 日 is U+65E5, 👍 is U+1F44D. The range runs to U+10FFFF, about 1.1 million values. The first 65,536 form the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP), which covers most living scripts; emoji and many historic scripts live above it. Unicode alone is just numbering; an encoding decides the bytes.

UTF-8 is variable length. Code points up to U+007F take one byte, 0xxxxxxx, identical to ASCII. Up to U+07FF take two bytes, 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx; up to U+FFFF take three, 1110xxxx then two continuation bytes; the rest take four, 11110xxx then three. The leading bits tell a decoder how long each sequence is, and continuation bytes always start 10, so a decoder dropped into the middle of a stream can find the next character. ASCII text is already valid UTF-8, no byte of a multi-byte character can be mistaken for an ASCII character such as / or a NUL, and there's no byte order to worry about. That's why UTF-8 is the encoding of the web, Linux and most files and APIs.

UTF-16 uses 16-bit code units. A BMP code point is one unit. A code point above U+FFFF becomes a surrogate pair: subtract 0x10000, put the top 10 bits in a high surrogate (0xD800 to 0xDBFF) and the low 10 bits in a low surrogate (0xDC00 to 0xDFFF). Those values are reserved, so they never stand for characters on their own. As bytes, UTF-16 needs a byte order: UTF-16LE writes the low byte first, and a byte order mark (U+FEFF) at the start can say which. Windows, Java and JavaScript chose 16-bit characters in the early 1990s, when Unicode still fit in 16 bits, and .NET followed Windows; that's why their strings are UTF-16 today.

So a string has at least three lengths. In C#, s.Length counts UTF-16 code units. Python 3's len(s) counts code points. Users count grapheme clusters, the things they see as one character: e followed by a combining acute accent (U+0301) is two code points shown as one é, and a family emoji is several emoji joined by zero-width joiners. In C#, StringInfo.LengthInTextElements counts graphemes and the Rune type steps through code points; Encoding.UTF8.GetByteCount gives the byte length that a database column or network buffer cares about.

Reversal shows why this matters. Reversing a C# char array swaps the two halves of a surrogate pair, leaving invalid lone surrogates. Reversing by code points keeps the emoji but moves a combining accent onto the wrong letter and pulls apart joined emoji. The correct answer is to reverse grapheme clusters. Also note that é can be one code point (U+00E9) or two (e plus U+0301): they look identical but compare unequal ordinally (code point by code point) until you normalize both with string.Normalize() (NFC). For how multi-byte numbers are ordered in memory, see Byte Order.
